Medical Chat — Pending Information Playbook
These people already paid. They finished the assessment, their card went through,
and then everything stopped — because the doctor asked them a question and
nobody answered it. No prescription can be written until they reply. You are the
reason they find out.
WHERE FILTER APPLIES TO CLOCK
Dosable → Subscriptions Subscription Status = Pending All verticals 7 days · work it in 5
Executive Summary
01
Every recovery playbook in this hub is about someone who almost bought. This one is about
someone who already did. They completed the health assessment, they went through
checkout, and the money is authorised on their card. The order is sitting in Pending — not
shipped, not even prescribed — for one reason only:
Page 1 of 22

THE WHOLE JOB IN ONE SENTENCE
The physician asked the patient something in the Medical Chat and the patient never
answered. You call them, tell them the doctor is waiting, and get them into their patient
portal to reply. That is the entire call. You never answer for them.
There are two things the doctor typically needs, and it changes the sentence you say — not the
call itself:
Identity could not be verified automatically. The system tried to match the patient against
public records and failed, so the medical team asked for a photo of a government-issued
ID — sent as a message in that same chat. Nothing suspicious is implied — it happens to
plenty of legitimate patients, often just a name or address that doesn't match exactly.
The physician needs more clinical information. Most commonly about medications the
patient is currently taking — an answer in the intake was left blank, or it contradicts
something else they wrote. The doctor will not prescribe without it.
WHY THE PATIENT HAS NO IDEA
The message is sitting inside the Medical Chat in their patient portal. Most people never log
back in after checkout. The notification email lands in spam, or it's read and forgotten. From
their side they paid for a treatment and nothing arrived — and the longer that goes on, the more
it looks to them like they were charged for nothing.
Why this queue matters more than it looks
The sale is already made. There is nothing to sell, no plan to pick, no price to negotiate.
Every one of these patients decided to buy and paid.
It is a hard clock, not a soft one. The card authorisation is only good for 7 days. Miss it and
the charge falls away — the patient gets nothing, Standard Meds collects nothing, and the
whole thing has to start over. See §2.
It is pure retention. A patient who paid and never received anything doesn't just churn —
they churn angry, and often as a chargeback.
Nobody else is doing it. The doctor asked once, in writing, and moved on. If you don't make
the call, that message is never read.
THE ONE BOUNDARY THAT RUNS THROUGH THIS ENTIRE PLAYBOOK
You are calling to tell someone a message is waiting and to help them go read it. You never
take the answer yourself. Not the ID photo, not the list of medications, not "just tell me and I'll
Page 2 of 22

pass it on." The physician needs it from the patient, sent in the patient's own Medical Chat. Full
rules in §7.
The Queue at a Glance
02
Where the list lives, what a row is telling you, and how long you have before the row is worth
nothing.
Dosable → Subscriptions → All Subscriptions
PENDING PRESCRIPTIONS · ONE TENANT PER VERTICAL · FILTERED BY HAND
Unlike the funnel-recovery lists, this queue isn't handed to you as a ready-made list. You build it
yourself in the Dosable dashboard with one filter, one vertical at a time. Step-by-step in §3.
WHO'S ON IT Patients who completed checkout and paid, but have not been prescribed,
because the medical team is waiting on something from them.
THE FILTER More Filters → Subscription Status → PENDING. That one checkbox is the
whole queue.
ONE TENANT AT A The dashboard shows one vertical at a time, chosen in the Select a tenant
TIME dropdown at the top right. There is no "all verticals" view — you work each
one in turn.
VERTICALS LIVE Neuropathy (NeuroCalmRx) · ED (QuattroRx · TriShot) · Anti-Aging / Skin
NOW (LiftRx) · Nail Fungus (ZoliraRx). Check every one — the same problem
happens in all of them.
ORDER ID The reference for that patient's order. Use it in your notes so Standard Meds
can find the exact case.
ORDER DATE Your clock starts here. Read it carefully — the dashboard shows times in
GMT-3, not the patient's local time.
TOTAL What they already paid. Worth glancing at: a $1,188 annual plan and a $99
month are the same call, but not the same loss if it expires.
DR STATUS Where the medical review stands. PENDING means no prescription has been
written.
THE CHAT ITSELF The row does not tell you what the doctor asked. You have to open each
patient's chat to find out — and to check whether they already replied. That is
Page 3 of 22

the actual work of building this list.
A ROW IN PENDING IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY A CALL
Some of these patients have already answered and are simply waiting on the doctor. Others
were never asked anything. Open the chat before you dial. Calling somebody to chase a
message they already replied to costs you their trust in the first ten seconds.
The 7-day clock — this is the part that actually matters
When the patient checks out, the charge is authorised, not captured: the money is held on
their card, waiting for the prescription. That hold is good for 7 days from the order date. If the
prescription hasn't been written by then, the authorisation expires and the money is released
back — the order is dead and cannot be rescued by answering the doctor afterwards. The
patient has to buy again from scratch, and almost nobody does.
HOW TO READ THE ORDER DATE
1 2 3 4
fresh fresh call now urgent
5 6 7
last call too late expiring
Target: everyone reached inside 5 days. The window is 7, but the last two days are not yours — the
patient still has to log in, find the chat, write the answer or upload the ID, and then the physician still
has to review it. Treat day 5 as the deadline and you leave the medical team room to actually finish.
WORK THE ONES ABOUT TO EXPIRE FIRST
Order the list by days left on the card authorization and start with the smallest number — day
6, then day 5, then day 4. A patient on day 6 is gone tomorrow whatever you do afterwards; a
patient on day 1 will still be there this evening. If you only get through half the list today, make
sure it's the half that can't wait.
This is the opposite of how you work a renewals list, and the difference is the deadline: a
declined renewal can be retried any time, but a card authorization that reaches day 7 simply
dies. Old here does not mean cold — it means nearly out of time.
Dispositions — what to set when the call ends
Same statuses you already use on the other queues:
Page 4 of 22

Recovered
They logged in and answered the doctor — the ID was uploaded or the question was replied to — while you
were on the line.
Callback scheduled
They will do it later, or they can't get to a phone or computer right now. Agree a time and note it — and
remember the clock.
Didn't reply
No answer, voicemail, or no contact made on this attempt.
Not interested
They no longer want the treatment and want the charge released. Respect it, note the reason, and pass it
to Standard Meds.
Organic
They had already answered the doctor before you called.
Lost
Unreachable, wrong number, or the order's window has already expired.
"RECOVERED" HERE MEANS ANSWERED, NOT APPROVED
Your win is the patient replying in the portal. What the physician decides afterwards is not
yours to promise or to predict — never tell a patient they are approved, only that the doctor
now has what they were waiting for.
Finding the Patients — Step by Step
03
Four steps in the Dosable dashboard, repeated once per vertical. Do this at the start of the shift
so you're calling a list, not hunting one patient at a time.
NAIL FUNGUS HAS ITS OWN SCREEN — START THERE, NOT HERE
For Nail Fungus, go to Subscriptions → All Pending instead. That list has two columns the
others don't — NAIL IMAGE and VISIT SENT — and they tell you which of the three cases you
Page 5 of 22

have before you open anything. Jump to the Nail Fungus branch below, then come back to Step
3.
STEP 1
Pick the vertical, then filter on Pending
Choose the vertical in Select a tenant (top right), go to Subscriptions → All
Subscriptions, open More Filters, then Subscription Status, and tick PENDING. Leave
everything else alone. The table now shows only orders that were paid but never
prescribed.
More Filters → Subscription Status → PENDING. Note the tenant selector top right — that's the
vertical. Sort by order date and work the oldest still inside the 7 days first — those are the ones
about to run out.
DO THIS FOR EVERY VERTICAL, EVERY DAY
There is no combined view. Neuropathy, ED, Anti-Aging (Skin) and Nail Fungus each
have their own tenant, and each one accumulates its own pending patients. A vertical
you skip is a day of orders nobody called.
STEP 2
Open the patient and press Open Chat
Click the order to open the patient's page. Confirm you're on the right person and take
the two things you need before dialling: which product they bought and what they
paid. Then press Open Chat on the right.
Page 6 of 22

The order page. Open Chat is in the Customer Detail panel on the right. Status PENDING and
AUTHORIZE on the item line is exactly the state this playbook is about — money held, nothing
prescribed.
STEP 3
Read the Doctor / Patient channel and decide if there's a call to make
The chat opens on Doctor / Patient, which is read-only for everyone but the doctor and
the patient — you can see it, you cannot write in it. Ignore the automated welcome
message at the top; you're looking for what came after it.
Doctor asked something and there is no reply below it → this is your call.
The patient already answered → no call. Disposition Organic and move on.
Nothing but the welcome message → the doctor hasn't asked anything yet. Not
your queue. Leave it.
Case A — identity. "We were not able to find an identity match based on the information that you
provided. Please send us a picture of your government-issued photo ID for verification."
Page 7 of 22

Unanswered, and the order is frozen behind it.
Case B — clinical information. The physician needs to know which medications the patient is on:
the intake said "none", then asked about interactions with current medications. He will not
prescribe until that's cleared up.
READ IT TO KNOW WHICH CALL YOU'RE MAKING — NEVER TO ANSWER IT
You open the chat so you can say the right sentence on the phone. You do not reply in
it, you do not read the doctor's clinical wording out loud line by line, and you never help
the patient decide what to answer. See §7.
STEP 4
Build the call list, then dial
Work through the pending rows of one vertical, note the ones with an unanswered
doctor message, then start calling — fewest days left on the card first. Take with you,
per patient: the order ID, the product, the order date (so you know which day of the 7
you're on) and which of the three cases it is. Calls go out on your own dialer —
Dosable is where the list and the chat live, nothing else.
LOG EVERY ATTEMPT AGAINST THE ORDER ID
Notes are shared with Standard Meds. Record what happened and what was agreed
against the order ID — that's what stops the same patient being called twice, and it's
what tells the medical team a reply is on its way.
Nail Fungus — read the two columns before you dial
Page 8 of 22

Pick the Standard Meds - Fungus tenant, then Subscriptions → All Pending. The list carries
two columns that decide everything: NAIL IMAGE and VISIT SENT. Read them left to right and
the case names itself.

Subscriptions → All Pending, Fungus tenant. Patient 1 is red on both columns — the photo never came,
so the visit never left. Patients 2 and 3 are green on both: their visits are with the doctor.
Both red — the nail photo is missing
Click the customer name to open the patient. On their page, top right, is Masquerade — it
opens the portal exactly as the patient sees it, so you can see what they're stuck on and walk
them through it while you have them on the phone.
Page 9 of 22

The customer page. Masquerade is top right. Send Login Link on the right panel re-sends the magic
login email — useful when the patient says they can't find theirs. Never use Reset Password: these
accounts have no password.
Masquerade lands straight on the box the patient has been ignoring: "Please select the image
that most closely resembles your affected nail(s)" — five reference photos plus Upload custom
image. Nothing else in the portal is reachable until this is done.
What the patient sees the moment they log in. One choice and NEXT — that is the entire blocker. Most
patients simply closed the tab at checkout and never came back.
THE PATIENT DESCRIBES THEIR OWN NAIL. YOU NEVER DECIDE FOR THEM.
Ask them what the nail looks like and read the options out — "which of these sounds closest to
yours?" — and let them choose. Better still, get them logged in on their own phone and let
them tap it. Never pick an image based on your own judgement, and never guess for a
Page 10 of 22

patient who isn't sure — that is clinical information going to a doctor with your opinion in it,
not theirs. If they can't decide, tell them to take a photo of the nail and use Upload custom
image; their own photo is always the right answer.
Both green, order still PENDING — the doctor asked something
Here the photo arrived and the visit went out. Click the subscription ID — not the name — to
open the order, then OPEN CHAT in the Customer Detail panel.
Both columns green and still on the pending list — that combination means the ball is with the patient.
Click the subscription ID on the left.
The order page. OPEN CHAT on the right. Note Visit — SENT lower down: that is the same fact the green
column told you, confirmed on the order itself.
Page 11 of 22

Two messages, and only the second one counts. The first is the automated welcome that every patient
gets. The real question is underneath it — here, a clinical one about the nails. Note the banner at the
bottom: view-only. You can read it; you cannot reply, and neither can Standard Meds.
EVERY PATIENT HAS TWO MESSAGES. THAT IS NOT THE SIGNAL.
The welcome message goes out automatically the moment the visit is sent, so a patient with
"two messages" may have had no real question at all. Read past the welcome. If there is
nothing after it, the doctor simply hasn't got to this order yet — there is no call to make and
nothing for the patient to do.
What the Doctor Is Waiting For
04
Three cases. Two of them end with the patient answering in the Medical Chat; the third never
gets that far, because the doctor has not seen the case at all. Read the third row first — it is the
one that looks like nothing is happening.

THE FRAMING THAT WORKS FOR ALL THREE
"The doctor needs a bit more information before he can go ahead with your prescription." That
is true in every case, it puts nobody on the defensive, and it makes the next step obvious. It is
also the only framing you need — you never have to explain identity matching, interaction
checks, or why we need to see the nail.
Where you're sending them — same portal, two different destinations
Everything happens in the patient's own portal: patient.standardmeds.com/login. There is no
password — the patient enters their email and gets a login link sent to them. What they see
once inside depends on which case they are.
1. Go to patient.standardmeds.com/login — the same email they used at checkout
2. They receive a login link by email — no password to remember
Page 13 of 22

3. Nail photo pending: the image box opens on its own, over the dashboard. Nothing else is
reachable until they pick an image and press NEXT. There is no chat to open and no doctor
message waiting — that is the whole point.
4. ID or clinical question: open Medical Chat in the top menu — the unread message is flagged
there. Reply with a photo of their ID or the answer in their own words, depending on what
was asked.
DON'T SEND A NAIL FUNGUS PATIENT LOOKING FOR A DOCTOR'S MESSAGE
If the nail photo is what's missing, there is no message in the chat and there never was —
the doctor cannot see the order until the visit is sent. Telling that patient to "check what the
doctor asked" sends them hunting for something that does not exist, and they hang up
believing the site is broken. Check which case you have before you dial: §03 shows you exactly
where to look.
TELL EVERY PATIENT TO WATCH THEIR EMAIL
Every time the doctor writes, the patient gets a notification email. Patients who never open the
portal again are the ones this queue is made of, so close every call the same way: "Keep an eye
on your email and on the portal — that's where the doctor talks to you, and it's what keeps your
treatment from being delayed."
THE LOGIN LINK GOES TO THEIR EMAIL — CHECK IT'S THE RIGHT ONE
If they say the link never arrives, ask them to check spam first, then confirm the email address
on the order matches the one they're checking. A typo in the email at checkout is a real and
common cause — if that's what it is, don't try to fix it on the call. Note it against the order ID
and pass it to Standard Meds.
YOU MAY SEND THEM THE PORTAL ADDRESS. THAT'S ALL YOU SEND.
Texting so they don't mistype it is fine and helps, and so is
patient.standardmeds.com/login
giving them if they're uneasy about putting their ID in the chat.
support@standardmeds.com
Never send anything else — no login codes, no links from your own systems. And never ask
them to send the ID photo to you, by text, by email or any other way. There are exactly two
places it may go: the Medical Chat, or the Standard Meds support inbox. Your own inbox is
never one of them.
Page 14 of 22

The Call Playbook
05
One stage, two flavours. Openers and questions are a guide, not a script to read verbatim.
Remember who's on the other end: somebody who paid for a treatment, heard nothing, and
may already be a little annoyed about it.
MEDICAL CHAT · SINGLE STAGE
Pending Information — Get Them Into the Portal
A paid patient whose prescription is frozen behind an unanswered question. Your tone is
service, not sales — nothing is being sold, nothing is being asked of them except a minute of
their time. The single best thing you bring to this call is the news that somebody is waiting on
them and they didn't know.
GOAL
Patient replies in the portal
AVG CALL
≤ 5 min
POSTURE
Helpful — never investigative
BEFORE YOU DIAL (30 SECONDS IN DOSABLE)
Which product they bought — name it correctly.
The order date, so you know which day of the 7 you're on.
Which case it is — identity, or clinical information (§4).
Whether the patient has already replied since the list was built.
OPENER (≤ 20 SEC)
"Hi {first name}, this is {agent name} calling from Standard Meds about your {product}
order. Everything's fine with your payment — the doctor just needs one more thing from
you before he can finish your prescription, and it's a two-minute fix. Have you got a
moment?"
FRAME IT (≤ 30 SEC)
"Your order's been sitting with the medical team since {order date}. The doctor sent you a
message in your patient portal and it hasn't been answered yet — most people never see
it, it's not just you. As soon as you reply, he can go ahead."
Page 15 of 22

CASE A — IDENTITY VERIFICATION
"He needs to confirm your identity before he can prescribe. The system couldn't match
your details automatically — that happens all the time, it's nothing to do with you. All he
needs is a photo of your driver's licence or another government ID. You upload it to him in
the medical chat in your account — attach the photo and send it like any other message."
Then:"It goes straight to the doctor from there — I never see it and it doesn't come through me."
That is true, and say it — it is the single best answer to a patient who is nervous about a
phone call asking for ID.
CASE B — CLINICAL INFORMATION
"He's got a question he needs you to answer before he can write the prescription — it's
about the medications you're currently taking. It's in the medical chat in your account. If
you log in and answer him there, he can move forward with it."
Then:"I can't answer it for you — it goes straight to the doctor and he needs it from you. But I can
stay on while you log in."
WALK THEM IN (THIS IS WHERE THE CALL IS WON)
Give them the address: patient.standardmeds.com/login. Spell it if needed, or text
it so they don't mistype it.
They enter the same email they used to order and get a login link by email — no
password. Warn them to check spam.
Nail photo pending (Nail Fungus): stop here — the image box opens by itself and
nothing else is reachable. They pick the closest photo (or upload their own) and
press NEXT. There is no chat to open; don't send them looking for one.
Everyone else:Medical Chat in the top menu — the unread message is flagged
there.
ID request: they attach a photo of their ID and send it as a message. Clinical
question: they type the answer in their own words.
Stay on the line. Read one step, wait, then the next. Someone who hangs up to "do
it in a minute" usually doesn't — and there are only so many days left.
ADDRESS — MOST COMMON PATTERNS
"I didn't get any message." → the normal case, not a complaint to defend against.
"You wouldn't have — it's inside your account rather than an email. That's exactly
why I'm calling."
"I already sent that." → thank them, check the chat while you're on the line. If it's
there, apologise for the extra call and disposition Organic. Never argue with a patient
about what they did or didn't send.
Page 16 of 22

"Why do you need my ID? Is something wrong?" → nothing is wrong. "It's a legal
requirement before a doctor prescribes — they have to know who they're prescribing
to. The automatic check just couldn't match you, which usually means a middle name
or an old address."
"Have I been charged?" → the charge is held, not taken, and it completes when
the prescription is written. Say it plainly and don't overexplain.
"I'd rather not put my ID in there." — or it simply isn't going through → don't argue
and don't troubleshoot an upload. "That's no problem at all — you can email it
instead, to support at standardmeds dot com, from the same email address you
ordered with. Our team puts it in front of the doctor for you." Chat first, email
whenever they're not comfortable with it; the photo still never comes to you.
"I'm not near a computer." → it works on a phone too. If they genuinely can't now,
book a specific time and set Callback scheduled — bearing in mind the window.
"Can't you just fix it on your end?" → no, and be straightforward about why. "It has
to come from you — the doctor can't accept it secondhand."
Anything clinical — is this drug safe with mine, what dose, should I be taking it →
stop. That is the physician's, and the chat is exactly where it belongs. "That's a great
question for the doctor — put it in that same chat and he'll answer you."
WHY IT'S WORTH THEIR MINUTE (USE IT IF THEY HESITATE)
CONTINUITY ANGLES — NO DISCOUNTS, NO
INVENTED OFFERS, NO PROMISES OF APPROVAL
They have already paid — this is the last step between them and the order they placed
Nothing has to be redone: no new assessment, no new checkout, the price and plan are
unchanged
It takes under two minutes, on the phone in their hand
The doctor is waiting on them right now — the review moves as soon as they reply
If nobody answers, the order eventually lapses on its own and they'd have to start over
CLOSE
"Shall we do it now while I'm on the line? I'll talk you through exactly where to
click."
CONFIRM BEFORE HANGING UP
"Perfect — that's gone through to the doctor. He'll review it and you'll hear about your
prescription from Standard Meds. Nothing else is needed from you and there's nothing
more to pay. Anything else I can help with?"
Page 17 of 22

Never say they're approved, tell them when they'll be approved, or estimate a shipping date. The
physician decides, and you don't speak for the physician.
VOICEMAIL SCRIPT
"Hi {first name}, this is {agent name} from Standard Meds. I'm calling about your recent
order — the medical team needs one more thing from you before it can go ahead, and it's
waiting in your account at patient dot standardmeds dot com. Nothing's wrong and there's
nothing more to pay. Please log in when you get a chance, or give us a call back. Thank
you!"
Note: never leave the product name, the medication, the condition, or the word "ID" on a voicemail —
you cannot know who listens to it. "Your recent order" is as specific as it gets.
Objection Library
06
Guidance, not scripts to read verbatim. Two hard boundaries run through all of it: anything
clinical goes to the physician in the chat, and anything about the money goes to Standard Meds
— you never improvise a refund, a credit or a discount.
Q "How do I know this is really Standard Meds and not a scam? You're asking for my ID."
A "Completely fair, and I'd rather you ask. I'm not asking you for your ID — I'm not going to take anything
from you over the phone. What I'm telling you is that there's a message waiting in your own account, and
you can go to the site yourself, log in the normal way, and see it. I'll wait while you check." (Never push
past this. A patient protecting their identity is doing the right thing.)
Q "Why can't I just tell you the answer / send you the photo?"
A "I know it would be quicker, and I wish I could. The doctor can't accept it through me — it has to come
from your account so it goes straight to him on the medical record. That's the whole reason it's set up
that way." (Hard rule — no exceptions, ever.)
Q "I'd rather not put my ID in that chat." / "It won't send."
A "That's no problem at all — you can email it instead. Send it to support at standardmeds dot com,
from the same email address you used to order, and our team will put it straight in front of the doctor for
you." (The chat is still what you ask for first, but the moment they're uncomfortable with it — or it just
isn't going through — offer the email rather than push. Applies to the ID photo only: a clinical answer —
medications, allergies, dose — has to be typed in the chat, because it belongs on the medical record in
the patient's own words. And it never comes to you: not to your inbox, not by text, not read out over the
phone.)
Page 18 of 22

Q "Have you taken my money?"
A "Not yet. The amount is held on your card and it only completes once the doctor writes the
prescription. That's actually why there's a bit of time pressure — the hold doesn't last forever."
Q "Why hasn't anyone told me this before?"
A "The doctor did message you, but it goes into the medical chat in your account rather than a normal
email, and almost nobody thinks to look there. That's exactly why we call."
Q "What's wrong with my ID? Am I being investigated?"
A "Nothing's wrong and nobody's investigating anything. Before a doctor prescribes, they have to
confirm who they're prescribing to. The automatic check couldn't match you — usually something as
small as a middle name, a recent move, or a maiden name. A photo of your licence clears it in a minute."
Q "Will the doctor definitely approve me once I do this?"
A "That's the doctor's decision and I genuinely can't speak for him. What I can tell you is that right now
he can't decide at all, because he's waiting on you." (Never promise approval. Not "you should be fine",
not "it's just a formality".)
Q "How long does it take after I answer?"
A "It goes to the medical team as soon as you send it and they review it in order. I don't want to give you
a date I can't stand behind — but nothing moves at all until they have it."
Q "I don't remember my password."
A "There isn't one — that's the good news. You put in the same email you ordered with and it sends you
a link to click. Have a look in spam if it doesn't land in a minute."

Compliance & Operational Rules
07
The universal rules from your first Standard Meds playbook still apply in full — calling window,
self-identification, recording disclosure, opt-out, no invented discounts, no claiming approval
before physician review. This section covers only what is different or elevated here — and this
queue carries a category the others don't, because you are standing next to identity documents
and clinical answers.
#1 RULE — YOU NEVER TAKE THE ANSWER
No ID photos. No identity details — no document numbers, no social security digits. No
list of medications. No "tell me and I'll pass it on." Not by phone, not by text, not to your
own email, not "just to check it's the right one". The patient sends it themselves, to one of two
places and no others: the Medical Chat, or — for an ID photo they'd rather not put in the chat
— support@standardmeds.com. If a patient sends you an ID photo or reads you an identity
number anyway, do not use it, do not store it, and report it — that is an incident.
New or elevated for this queue
Never answer the doctor's question for them
Not the medications, not the allergies, not the dose. You must not suggest an answer, hint at a "right"
answer, or help them remember. A prescription written on a coached answer is a patient safety problem,
not a save.
Never write in the Medical Chat
The Doctor / Patient channel is read-only to you by design. You read it to know which call you're making.
You never reply in it, on the patient's behalf or your own.
Never promise approval or a ship date

"You'll be approved", "it's just a formality", "it'll ship this week" — all forbidden. The physician decides and
no one else speaks for them. Your promise is only that the doctor will have what he asked for.
Never imply suspicion
An identity check that didn't match is not an accusation and must never sound like one. No "we need to
verify you're who you say you are", no "fraud", no "flagged". The system couldn't match their details —
that's the whole story.
Never discuss the order with a third party
If a spouse, relative or assistant answers, you may say you're calling from Standard Meds about an order.
You may not name the medication, the condition, or that a medical question is outstanding. Ask for the
patient or offer a callback. This is a HIPAA line.
Never leave clinical detail on a voicemail
No product name, no condition, no mention of ID or medical questions. "Your recent order" and a callback
number. You don't know who plays the message back.
Always confirm identity before anything else
Name and the email on the order, at minimum, before you discuss why you're calling. You are calling about
somebody's medical treatment — being on the wrong call is the worst outcome available.
Always send them to the real portal address
patient.standardmeds.com/login and nothing else. Never a shortened link, never a link from your own
tooling, never a login code. Patients are rightly suspicious of a phone call about their ID — the fact that
they can go to the site themselves is your best proof you're genuine.
Always check the chat before you dial
A patient who already answered and gets chased anyway loses confidence in the whole operation. Thirty
seconds of reading beats a bad first ten seconds on the phone.
Always log against the order ID
What happened, what was agreed, when to call back, and any broken email address you found. Never the
ID details, never anything the patient told you about their health.
HEALTH INFORMATION YOU HEAR STAYS WHERE YOU HEARD IT
Patients will tell you things on this call — what they take, what they've been diagnosed with,
why they're nervous. Do not write it in the notes, do not repeat it back, and do not pass it on
other than "the patient has a question for the doctor". The place for it is the chat, from them.
